title: Christopher Nolan on his career, including Oppenheimer and the Batman triology | BFI in conversation
transcript:
SPEAKER_A: So let's just start with a little bit of the kind of your essential love of film and the films that you saw, the films that really
made an impression on you and first gave you that feeling that, of what cinema could do and also maybe gave you an inkling of what you might be able to do in cinema.
SPEAKER_B: Yeah, I mean, I think the
first film I actually remember going to see, I was very young, was "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs." At, I think it was the Muswell Hill Odeon, which is now an Everyman, might've been the Holloway Odeon. And I remember very clearly
being affected by it, in particular the scene where the evil queen turns into
an old crone, you know? The poison apple, being
very frightened of that and sort of hiding behind the seats. I think as far as influential movies and things that sort of just
show me the potential of films, it was a very special time
in terms of blockbusters. So George Lucas' first "Star Wars" was, came out when I was seven years old. And "The Spy Who Loved Me" was
the Bond film at the time. I remember going to
see that in the cinema, and those are the kind
of films that I think a lot of filmmakers, you know, you come to film through
the Hollywood blockbuster. Those are the big films that, you know, as a kid you wind up going to see. I did have a very special
experience of going to see "2001" on a film print. Because "Star Wars" was so successful, they re-released that
film the year after that, so I went to see that with
my dad in Leicester Square at the old Leicester Square Theatre on, it would've been on 70 mil. And that was a film, I remember that experience very clearly. I remember just feeling
the enormity of the imaging and the potential for that
screen to kind of, you know, just take you anywhere, yeah.
SPEAKER_A: And I guess seeing it at that age, it's a, or indeed any age with "2001", it's, it is a question
of you experiencing it rather than understanding
every frame of it. It's a kind of cumulative
effect, isn't it?
SPEAKER_B: I think, I mean, I saw it
when I was seven years old and I think I understood
it certainly as well then as I do now, maybe better. (audience laughs) I think maybe better because you just, you take it for granted. You experience it and the beauty and the magnitude of the
images and the feeling of, you know, travelling across
the solar system or whatever. I mean, that's the point of the film. It's a sort of wood for the trees thing. I think as a kid, you're
actually pretty open to those visceral experiences and I think a lot of your
appreciation of movies and the entertainment value
of movies is very simple and it's just experiential
in that way, yeah.
SPEAKER_A: Did you also appreciate film as a kind of time machine as well? In that it sort of, it does
capture and transcend time. It can, you know, somebody
can die over and over again in film, can't they?
SPEAKER_B: They can indeed, yeah. I mean, I think some
years ago it was doing a, an event in India with my
friend, the artist Tacita Dean, who works on 60 millimetre film and has been very involved
with me and with the BFI in film preservation. That is to say, trying to
preserve the medium of film for future generations for
acquisition and for projection. And she pointed out that the
camera literally sees time and the more I thought
about what she said, and I applied it to my own fascinations and my own interest in it for work, I mean, you know, it's
only in a post-film world where you can conceive of
slow motion or fast motion or things running backwards, you know? These are things that people
before movies wouldn't have had any idea of or any thought of.
SPEAKER_A: And was that, so that was something
that you first appreciated through film rather, 'cause it was literature that
you studied at university, but it was film that.
SPEAKER_B: I did but I mean, I
mostly was making films and, you know, thinking
about films, you know? Getting by in literature. But yeah, I mean, my interest
in films has always been sort of overwhelming in terms
of anything else going on in my life. And when I got to UCL,
where I went to college, there was a film society,
a student-run film society in the basement of Bloomsbury Theatre. It's still there today. And you were able to
shoot 16 millimetre films and then in the Bloomsbury
Theatre upstairs, we would project 35 millimetre films and use the proceeds from
that to pay for filmmaking. So even though I was, yes, I was studying English literature, I think I spent most of my
time making films, actually.
SPEAKER_A: And clearly, you were
attracted to film noir as a early on, as a.
- Mm.
SPEAKER_B: Because, which I suppose
is a kind of expression of the human psyche, isn't it? As much as being any, having any kind of thriller content and film noir and psychoanalysis
kind of grew up together grappling, didn't they?
SPEAKER_A: Yeah, I, no, I think to a degree, yeah. I mean, I think film noir certainly, I think the attraction of that genre, particularly to a younger
filmmaker starting out as it is, it works at its best as an extrapolation of relatable fears and anxieties. And that's really the
bedrock of the attraction of that genre for audiences. And so when you're younger, starting out, and you don't know anything,
haven't experienced anything, being able to extrapolate from
your own fears and anxieties into a more universal realm, a more universal language, that's a really important
tool for a filmmaker.
SPEAKER_B: So when you came to make "Memento", which was, I mentioned
following in the introduction, which had obviously a noir kind of, the step then to "Memento",
which was, as it were, the breakthrough film, again, very much a kind
of noir but about memory in some ways, in a very complex sense. So what made you want to
make a film, as it were, where the chronology was backwards?
SPEAKER_A: Well I think, you know, in the noir tradition there is
a tradition of amnesic films that "Memento" was certainly
inspired by and tapping into, but it's based on a short
story that my brother wrote and told me about as he
was writing, in fact. And it, yeah, I mean, it's essentially
dealing with somebody who can't make new memories. And ultimately what we decided, what I decided in talking
to my brother about it and tasked him with him
finishing his story, is if you could tell
the story subjectively, that would surely be the
most interesting way of, you know, trying to live in
somebody's head like that. And so he in his story
found ways to approach that. And me in the screenwriting, you know, ultimately decided that if
you inverted the chronology, you know, then you'd put
yourself in the position of somebody who doesn't
know what's just happened. I mean, the revenge story is, you know, it's a staple of movies
and literature generally, and noir fiction in particular. And so it always raises
interesting ethical questions. And I think "Memento", more
than any film I've made, really tries to suggest
that the ethical framework of the dilemma is defined
really by the point of view. So it really is a question of
whether you are in his head or whether you are
observing him from outside in terms of how you judge the
ethics of how he's behaving.
SPEAKER_B: So following on from
"Memento", you made "Insomnia", which was, had originally been, there was a Norwegian film, and this is, this was the.
- Mm.
SPEAKER_A: Hollywood version of this. So you were working at that stage from somebody else's script, which is you then you're
done with that after that. But I suppose "Insomnia"
still felt a bit like you know, you were dealing with something that's originally been a
kind of art house film, but then you go to the
"Dark Knight" trilogy, which that's introduced you
obviously to Warner Bros., and then you go to the
"Dark Knight" trilogy. Was that a big decision, to go from something, because you'd made such
personal films until then? I know you were still starting out. Was that something that you
and Emma Thomas discussed as, you know, what you should do next?
SPEAKER_B: No, not really. I mean, I think the notion
of personal or not personal doesn't really apply to my work. They're all equally personal and actually, I mean the
interesting thing with "Insomnia" was it was a remake of, yeah, a very brilliant Norwegian film. And Hillary Seitz, who is
credited with the screenplay, she had written a great
adaptation of the original film and then she worked with me. I was a great creative
partner in rewriting. I then did the last draught myself. I didn't take a credit because
she had done, you know, the vast majority of the work,
so that seemed appropriate. But I did write the last draught, and I do on all of my films. And so my relationship
with the material is no different really than any other film I've been involved with because
some of them are adaptation, some of 'em are original, that one's a remake,
some have been sequels, some are from novels, you know? I mean, it's always different. And yet the process has
to be always the same in terms of finishing that last draught and then me approaching it as a director. So no, I think where you see
a more specific progression, and that was probably a little more not necessarily self-conscious, but the scale of the films, you know, grows in what for me was
a very useful cadence because it went from a no budget film, you know, "Following" was
literally made, you know, with friends, shooting on the weekend, we were all working,
you know, full-time jobs and it was made for nothing. And then "Memento" was a,
you know, a low-budget movie, but you know, it was
about $4 million or so. And then "Insomnia" was
sort of 10 times that. So then by the time we get
to the "Dark Knight" trilogy, starting with "Batman Begins", you're working on a much bigger scale. But it was a pretty good
progression, actually. So I felt I was challenged at every stage with taking on something bigger, but I didn't do what a lot of
filmmakers since, you know, I did those films, there've been a lot of
filmmakers who've gone from their sort of
whatever their "Memento" is straight to their "Batman Begins". And that's a very difficult leap. And I would not have wanted
to have to try and make that kind of technical leap in terms of marshalling
resources and everything. I feel very lucky to have done a more modestly budgeted studio film and learned a lot about
how to make that work and working within that system
before I then, you know, took on their larger scale properties.
SPEAKER_A: And your vision for Gotham
City and Bruce Wayne's travails was informed quite a lot by
sort of European expressionism, by Fritz Lang, I mean.
SPEAKER_B: Yeah, definitely. I mean, I think Lang's influence was more on "The Dark Knight", actually. I think with "Batman
Begins" on the design, working with Nathan Crowley,
who worked with for years, we, he very much wanted to take
it in a modernist direction, and I liked that and enjoyed that, and we pushed a little
bit in that direction. But I felt that given
the history of Batman, how he'd been portrayed on film before, even though we were trying
to do something different, I didn't wanna completely abandon the sort of gothic underpinnings
of it quite so much. And so "Batman Begins" was
more of a hybrid in that sense. And then by the time we
got to "The Dark Knight", we'd sort of built more confidence to take it in our own direction and push in a very heavily, sort of modern, modernist direction. And for the script more
than the design really, I pushed my brother, who wrote the first draught
of "The Dark Knight", I pushed him very much in
the direction of Fritz Lang, look at "Dr. Mabuse" and things like that, this idea of the sort of
master criminal in, you know, expressionist cinema, the relationship between the
city and the master criminal. And I think it gave him a
lot of inspiration, actually. I think visually, that isn't necessarily as strong a relationship. I think it's a little bit
more about almost sort of the morality of the thing really, and the relationship between
police and, you know, criminal underworld and then the idea of some kind of geographical or architectural
expression of that within the visual nature of the film. But obviously, we're doing it in a more modern way, I suppose.
SPEAKER_A: And also the kind of
Faust themes as well in that Bruce Wayne takes
on this mantle of Batman at some considerable
personal cost, doesn't he? There's a price.
SPEAKER_B: Yeah, definitely. Well, it's, yeah, it is a
sort of deal with the devil. I mean, it's really that idea of a sort of means
to an end, if you like. And I think the Batman mythology, one of the reasons that
it's continually interesting and is continually
reinvented by new generations of comic book writers and
artists and filmmakers is because that essential paradox or that essential idea of
a good vigilante, you know, somebody who feels that
they have to resort to criminal methods or
be outside the system in order to fix the system, it's endlessly complex and
interesting in its ethics.
SPEAKER_A: And also the sort of twinning theme, which will turn up in
your films, you know, before and after, that idea is if there's a
Batman, there should be a Joker. Were you surprised by the appeal
of the Joker to audiences, how fascinated they were by him?
SPEAKER_B: I mean no, I wasn't, because when I read Jonah's first draught, which was, it was a
very unwieldy document, and it, you know, it was long and took us a long time to kind of get it into a practical shape, but the character of the Joker was there, like this sort of engine
running through it. I had told him I needed the Joker to be like the shark in "Jaws". He needed to sort of come through, a thread through the film in this, with this particular energy. And he had just found that
and absolutely cracked that even in that first draught. And then when I brought Heath on and talked about it and how it was gonna
work and saw his ideas and his references, and as
that started to come together, it was endlessly fascinating. You know, very, very interesting to see. And as we shot with Heath, you know, right from the first hair and makeup test, you could see everybody on the
floor just fascinated by it. I mean, it was just such a
sort of interesting creation and it started with Jonah's script and then Heath's interpretation
was so compelling that now I think we all felt
as we were filming it that that character would have
very, very special appeal. And I think the challenge
actually of the film and the edit was to have
all of the other elements in balance with that. So, you know, Christian Bale,
Gary Oldman, everything, you know, their story, you know, you can't give it all over to the Joker, even though he's this incredibly magnetic and powerful force at the centre of it. But no, I think we all sort of felt that really developing as we
were making the film.
SPEAKER_A: Yeah, I guess that the challenge is that billionaire Bruce Wayne is, you know, in some ways a less attractive figure.
SPEAKER_B: Yes.
- You know, in cinematic terms than.
SPEAKER_A: Well, but I mean a good villain, I mean, the devil has
the best tunes, you know? That's the thing. And it's what really, as I say, it's the engine of the film, it's what really makes it work. So we all knew how important
it was going to be, but it was thrilling to see audiences really, really respond to that.
SPEAKER_B: And of course, there've been
all sorts of interpretations from right or left about
appropriating the Joker one way or another. I mean, what do you make of those?
SPEAKER_A: Politically speaking?
- Yeah.
SPEAKER_B: Well, I mean we found
that on all three films, people often attempting to put some kind of political
interpretation on the films, but it sort of ignores
the mythic landscaping which should take place, certainly with "The Dark Knight Rises", which, you know, has its
share of people pulling at it politically right and left. Either side of the political spectrum in choosing to interpret
the film in their own terms, they're willfully ignoring, you know, big chunks of the story to do that, or big chunks of the point of view. So really, it's important to
remember the mythic landscape. The end of "The Dark Knight"
is really drawn from "Shane", the Western, you know, George
Stevens' wonderful Western, and out of the past, you know,
so it's mythic Americana, it's film noir, it's the Western. I think where people get
slightly confused by it all in that sense is that it's
a contemporary staging, because that's what works for Batman. But even though it's a recognisable sort of contemporary American cityscape, emotionally, you know, thematically, it's the mythic Americana of, you know, crime fiction and of the Western.
SPEAKER_A: I mean, nonetheless, it, the films did anticipate the rise of kind of disruptor leaders in politics all around the world, didn't they? So do you think they were
sort of their time in that?
SPEAKER_B: Oh, I think they very much, yeah, very much of their time in that I mean, certainly with
David Goyer, my co-writer, with my brother Jonah, my other co-writer, the attempt was always to just be honest about presenting the
things we were affected by, things we were worried about, afraid of. I mean, certainly when I
look back at "Batman Begins", there's a heavy emphasis on terrorism, on the sort of post-9/11 world. But we, it wasn't something we were consciously putting into the film. We were just trying to
be sincere and truthful about what moved us at the time. Certainly, the Joker for
me and "The Dark Knight" is all about a fear of anarchy, you know, fear of the rules breaking down and what that would do to society. And "The Dark Knight Rises" is
very much fearful of fascism, fearful of demagoguery, and yeah, and I think, you know, I suppose in a sense we were
sort of tuning into things around us in the world
that we were worried about and you know, some of them
come to pass, you know?
SPEAKER_A: So obviously you made other films during that trilogy as well. Did the fantastic success, I mean, the huge box office takings of those films allow you to do something
like "Inception", for example, which, you know, is very
daring, cinematically?
SPEAKER_B: Yeah, I mean, it definitely helped. Yeah. (audience laughs)
SPEAKER_A: Sure.
- I mean, coming off "The Dark Knight", I think I'd been working on "Inception" for a very long time. I'd never really tried sort
of pitching it to the studio or anything, so I'd never
really gauged the response in the absence of "The Dark Knight". I'd probably been afraid to. But certainly following that film, when I took it to the
studio, they, you know, they were very receptive. They wanted to do another film with us, so that smoothed the way for
what might otherwise have been received with some raised eyebrows because it is a, it's an unusual film
and a complicated film and a very expensive film, which is a tricky combination. And so I think both Emma, myself, Emma Thomas, my producer and wife, who's somewhere in the audience here, I'm gonna single her out,
she's gonna stand up. Ah, there she is.
- There she is. (audience applauds)
SPEAKER_B: I think we both felt
coming off "The Dark Knight" that we had a very,
very unusual opportunity to make something on a
large scale with, I mean, not carte blanche, but
with a lot of freedom. And so we sort of dove in
headfirst to do "Inception" because you are very aware when you get an opportunity like that. I mean, firstly how much
you yourself wanted to do something very ambitious like that, but also how many other
filmmakers there are in the world who don't have that opportunity. So, you really feel, you know, kind of an obligation almost to just take a risk and maximise it.
SPEAKER_A: Can I bring in something
else that obviously was happening around the time in
terms of thinking about IMAX as a format?
- Mm.
SPEAKER_B: 'Cause clearly, you know, you're getting into an
area where these films are just extraordinary, that, was it something that you had in mind when you go to make a film? Are you thinking about
that particular format?
SPEAKER_A: Yeah, depending on the film. I had first experienced IMAX as a kid in museums around the world. Actually, OmniMax, which
is the variant of IMAX, it's a domed theatre that isn't, there's not much of it around anymore. But in various museums in
America, they had this format. You'd watch nature
documentaries and things. And I always found it
to be a very visceral, sort of overwhelming
experience and thought well, why not make a film that way? And as I started to get into film, there was no way to do that. But right around, you know, in the sort of 10 years
leading up to "Batman Begins", you know, when I was in my early 20s, IMAX started showing, they created a process
called the DMR process whereby they could take
a regular 35 mil film and blow it up for their screens. So they started building IMAX theatres in commercial cinemas for the first time. And so by the time we
got to "Batman Begins", I was able to say to the studio, "Well, can we transfer this?" We couldn't shoot in IMAX, no one had ever shot a thing
in IMAX for those screens, but then you had to transfer it. And so I got to meet the IMAX guys blowing up "Batman Begins" and you know, it did well in that format. So leading up to "The Dark Knight", I went to them and said, "I'd like to take your cameras," that have been used for you know, nature documentaries and, you know, they'd gone to outer
space and up Mount Everest and all this sort stuff, but no one had ever shot a
narrative feature with them. And so we started looking into it and it was a very large undertaking because no one had done it. There were a lot of unknowns,
a lot of fears about it. But I had read an interview
with James Cameron years before where he had talked about whether you could make a film on IMAX and how that would work in
terms of what he'd figured out, Cameron being the technical genius he is, is that you'd extract
from the larger negative the smaller negative that you'd need for your regular release. So rather than doing different
versions or whatever, you'd have one definitive version that you could transfer to your
other distribution formats. And that stuck in the back of my head. So when we came to do
it on "The Dark Knight", we figured out how to do that, how to shoot an IMAX negative, which is a, you know, very tall frame, but frame within that, protect for a CinemaScope version, which is like the clip we just showed. And make it work in that way and figure out which sequences
we could shoot that way. The cameras are very loud, so you don't really want to
do dialogue scenes that way. So we laid out which of
the action set pieces we would shoot with the IMAX camera, starting with the opening of the film where we introduced the Joker. And yeah, we went ahead and did that and it was you know, it was a great success and kind of moved the format forwards and I've been working in
that format ever since 'cause I just love it.
SPEAKER_B: And that's really where
the film begins with you, with the IMAX version, is it? I mean, is that what you're
thinking, as it were?
SPEAKER_A: I mean, yes and no. It depends on which sequences you are in. It's pushed us over the years, certainly working with Hoyte van Hoytema as I had, have for the
last 10 years or so, by the time we get to "Oppenheimer", our conversations are a lot about not, it pushes you to a way
of looking at cinematography where you're not looking
at the proscenium, you're not looking at the frame and making two dimensional compositions. You are really just putting the camera in proximity to the actors and you're composing in a
three dimensional sense. You're sort of composing situationally and then that gets formatted
to different shape screens and holds up great. And Hoyte has a wonderful eye for that. So in its IMAX version, the extreme top and bottom, it's really about the peripheral vision. It's really kind of filling out the frame rather than boxing it in. So it's less a question of seeing things get boxed into particular compositions and more a question of
pulling the frame away for that version. And so it translates, I think, very well to the other formats as
well for that reason. So, yeah, no, it's been a sort of ongoing experiment
that we quite enjoy.
SPEAKER_B: And moving on, as we
inevitably have to do given the constraints of time, to "Interstellar", there was a treatment by
the physicist Kip Thorne, I believe, which is sort of the basis, is it where you start, which is to do with relativity and gravity and well, all of those things. Is that where you began, and there was?
SPEAKER_A: Well, Kip, no, I mean, Kip had an ambition to, the genesis of the project
was Kip had an ambition to see a Hollywood film made
based on scientific principles. And so he was friends with
the producer, Lynda Obst and they had sort of taken
this idea to Steven Spielberg. And Steven hired my brother to write it. And so for years, I was aware of Jonah
developing this project, writing about it, so he would talk to me about it and I thought it was
pretty, pretty exciting. And then ultimately, Steven moved on and did something else, and so it became available
and I went to Jonah and said, "You know, how would
you feel if I took this and combined it," I had a couple other script ideas that I wanted to combine it with, and he was willing to sort
of, you know, let me do that. And then we managed to
negotiate with the studio so that we could take it on. And that's kind of where the, you know, the project really came from. And in the finished film, you know, the whole setup, the whole world of it, the whole first act is pretty unchanged from what Jonah developed over the years. And I worked very closely with Kip, who'd worked with my brother. And then when I took it over,
I worked closely with him as well to try and really
mine his incredible brain for what are the possibilities of science? What do concepts of relativity
offer you for a narrative? And Jonah had identified
early on in talking to Kip and researching it, he looked at a lot of Einstein's, Albert Einstein's sort
of thought experiments. They tend to be very narrative, so they tend to involve
a set of twins, you know, and one goes off on a
spaceship or whatever, one goes off on a train and
one is left at the station and they come back in the different ages and there's this sort of weird
melancholy to them almost. And so a lot of that fed into his idea of what the story should be. And then I just kind of
burrowed in, you know, further and further with Kip on the relationship between quantum physics and classical physics and, you know, gravitational theory and all this stuff. A lot of what, you know, he came back with was truly
stranger than fiction, really mind-blowing stuff. In visual terms, it found its ultimate expression in the look of the black
hole in "Interstellar", which Kip insisted he wanted to talk to the visual effects guys
about it and everything. And I sort of was a bit worried about that because ultimately, you want something that kind of looks cool. You don't necessarily. (audience laughs) It doesn't really matter if
it's scientifically accurate, but what Kip had figured out, Kip had all of the
equations that would explain you know, that would define how the gravitational
effect of the black hole would affect the light behind it and how it would therefore look. He just really needed the computing power of our visual effects
company to render that. So he worked very closely
with Paul Franklin, our visual effects supervisor, and they created this incredibly realistic rendering of a black hole. They actually published a couple of different scientific
papers jointly about it. And then some years later, they actually managed to
photograph a black hole in real life and it was on the front
of "The New York Times". And I looked at it and I called Kip and I said, "Well, I
guess you were right." (audience laughs) "Very glad to see that you were right and our black hole holds up," and yeah, it's sort of become
the kind of standard way of looking at it now, but it was all based on
absolutely the real science.
SPEAKER_B: So it's all moving towards "Oppenheimer" I guess, isn't it? In the sense of.
- Mm.
SPEAKER_A: Wanting to make that story of the father of the atom bomb and the discovery of that force to make us feel as though
we're there for it. Is that right?
SPEAKER_B: I think, yeah. I mean, I think with all my films I've had an increasing desire
to really try and create an immersive experience and try and create a tactile sense of a world and, you know, put you there in it. And I think that where that finds its, maybe its ultimate utility
in "Oppenheimer" is the excitement or the
tension of that story was always gonna be based on, you know, can you actually be there
for the Trinity test? Can you be in that room
with these scientists deciding to go ahead and do this thing and experience those stakes? Because obviously, it's a
story that's ultimately, it's about, you know,
people talking in rooms. It's not the most obviously cinematic, but the Trinity test itself in particular, if you can really feel that
you are there for that, it would've been just the
most extraordinary moment in history, you know, to be there and the tension of that, you know? It felt like it would be inarguable. And so yeah, I think I
brought my experience to bear in terms of creating that tension, creating that sense of being there. There's a lot of detailed
work and things that go into you know, feeling the tension around it, feeling that you're there. As I pointed out to Jen Lame, my editor, it's the second film done with her, but I said, "The thing I've
learned about editing suspense is it's very tedious to edit, actually, because you have to repeat things a lot." You have to sort of keep
showing the same thing advancing at a particular pace, and you have to tune that
pacing to the audience. And so Lee Smith, who cut
the clip we've just seen in "Interstellar", there's a lot of work on
how slow to make the robot relative, you know, to the
wave coming and all the rest. And you have to be very
mechanical and pedantic about how you put those sequences together so that the audience can understand what they need to for the tension.
SPEAKER_A: And those are things that
you can gauge in what way? I mean, how do you know what is the point where the audience will
become incredibly frustrated because a door is, a lever
is not moving or something?
SPEAKER_B: Well, I think you have to feel it with your own internal clock, and then you sit with an
audience and you watch it and that sort of tells you as well. But one of the things I've
learned over the years is to really judge it, you have to watch the whole film because your sense of internal rhythm is very, very different depending
on where you are in the film and the pace of the
sequence you've come out of. You know, I often have the experience, particularly with "The Dark Knight" films, if they're playing on TV or whatever and I happen to turn it on and
it's in the last third or so, the editing seems bizarrely fast to me. And you know, it's somewhat choppy because it has to be to get that pace, but it works if you watch
it from the beginning. So, it modulates through the film. You can't edit things with the same rhythm at different points in a
